name: Mr. Heater Portable Buddy Propane Heater
summary: The go-to indoor emergency heater for most households: it warms one closed-off room, it is easy to run, and it carries the safety devices that matter.
verdict: When people talk about indoor propane heat, the Portable Buddy, model MH9BX, is usually the heater they have in mind. Mr. Heater rates it at 4,000 or 9,000 BTU per hour and markets it as indoor-safe. In practice that means two devices: an oxygen depletion sensor that shuts the burner off if oxygen in the room falls, and a tip-over switch that kills the flame if the heater gets knocked over. Those two features are the reason it made this list and a patio heater did not. It burns a single 1-lb propane cylinder. Working from the fuel math, a 1-lb cylinder holds a little over 21,000 BTU, which comes to roughly two to two and a half hours on high and about five on low, so low is the setting you will really live on. Run it in a room you have closed off, open a window or door to the size the manual calls for, keep it at least the stated distance from bedding and curtains, and never light it without a working CO alarm in the same room.
skipIf: On high, a 1-lb cylinder lasts only a few hours, so keep a deep supply
pros: Mr. Heater sells it as indoor-safe, fitted with an oxygen depletion sensor and a tip-over shutoff
Two heat settings: low to carry you through the night, high to warm up a cold room
Rated for roughly 225 square feet, about the size of a typical bedroom
Burns a 1-lb propane cylinder and needs no electricity whatsoever
Piezo ignition and a fold-down handle make it simple to light and set in place
cons: On high, a 1-lb cylinder lasts only a few hours, so keep a deep supply
The manual requires a fresh-air opening, which lets some heat escape
The front grille runs hot enough to burn skin and scorch fabric

name: Mr. Heater Big Buddy Propane Heater
summary: Choose it when the warm room is a living room rather than a bedroom, or when the whole household is bunking together in one space.
verdict: Think of the Big Buddy, model MH18B, as a scaled-up Portable Buddy. Mr. Heater lists three settings, 4,000, 9,000 and 18,000 BTU, along with the same oxygen depletion sensor and tip-over shutoff, and it holds two 1-lb cylinders on board. Its rating covers spaces up to roughly 450 square feet, enough for a living room or a den where a family can gather with mattresses on the floor. The high setting exists to bring a cold room up to temperature, not to run all night. At 18,000 BTU an hour, two 1-lb cylinders last only a little over two hours by the fuel math, and the manual asks for a bigger fresh-air opening at higher output. Drop to low or medium once the room is warm. The fan genuinely helps in a larger room, and because it runs on D batteries it keeps working with the grid down. If your plan centers on one bedroom, the smaller Portable Buddy is easier and cheaper to keep fueled.
skipIf: The high setting burns fuel quickly and calls for more ventilation
pros: Three settings reaching 18,000 BTU, enough for a living room or open family area
Indoor-safe rating, with an oxygen depletion sensor and a tip-over shutoff
Carries two 1-lb cylinders, about doubling the time between swaps
An optional battery-powered fan spreads warmth across a larger room
cons: The high setting burns fuel quickly and calls for more ventilation
Larger and heavier than the Portable Buddy
More heater than a single bedroom needs

name: Mr. Heater Little Buddy Propane Heater
summary: A sensible heater for a small room and a useful backup unit, but its output is too low to be the only heat source in most homes.
verdict: Of the indoor-rated heaters in the Buddy line, the Little Buddy, model MH4B, is the smallest. Mr. Heater lists it at 3,800 BTU an hour for spaces up to about 95 square feet, with the same oxygen depletion sensor and tip-over protection as its siblings. The cylinder threads into the base, leaving a unit roughly the size of a large coffee can on a stand. The low output is deliberate. At 3,800 BTU an hour, a 1-lb cylinder runs for roughly five to six hours by the fuel math, enough to carry a small bedroom through much of the night with a single swap. It also suits a bathroom where you only need enough warmth to wash, or works as a second unit beside a Portable Buddy. In real cold it cannot keep up with a large room, and with no high setting it cannot recover a room that has already slipped into the 40s. Read the manual for altitude limits, since oxygen depletion sensors are sensitive to thin air.
skipIf: Only one heat setting, with no high option
pros: Compact and light, threading directly onto a 1-lb cylinder
Same oxygen depletion sensor and tip-over shutoff as the larger Buddy models
Modest 3,800 BTU output makes one cylinder last through more of the night
Sized for a bathroom, a small bedroom or a tent
cons: Only one heat setting, with no high option
The cylinder sits beneath it, so it stands tall and needs a stable, level surface
Not enough output for anything bigger than a small room

name: First Alert CO400 Battery-Powered Carbon Monoxide Alarm
summary: Buy this before any heater. Every fuel-burning heat source in a living space needs a working battery CO alarm right beside it.
verdict: A hardwired CO alarm with no battery backup falls silent as soon as the power drops, which is precisely when people start bringing fuel-burning equipment indoors. The First Alert CO400 runs on batteries, so the state of the grid does not matter to it. It uses an electrochemical sensor and, as UL 2034 alarms are designed to do, sounds a loud alarm when carbon monoxide builds to a dangerous concentration over time. It is the least expensive insurance on this page and the item that matters most. Place one in the room where the heater runs, one in or near each sleeping area, and one on every level of the house. Test it before the season begins and again ahead of any outage you can see coming. Kidde and other brands sell equivalent battery-powered alarms, and some add a digital display showing lower levels before the alarm threshold, a useful extra if you can find one. The essentials are that it runs on batteries and that it sits in the room.
skipIf: No digital display, so low but rising levels stay invisible
pros: Runs on batteries, so it keeps protecting you through the outage
Its electrochemical sensor triggers a loud alarm at dangerous CO levels
Compact enough to sit in the exact room where the heater runs
Cheap enough to buy one for every sleeping area
cons: No digital display, so low but rising levels stay invisible
The alarm and its batteries have a limited service life; replace them on schedule

specs.Features: Battery CO Alarm, Works Without Grid Power

atAGlance: Battery CO Alarm, Works Without Grid Power

name: Sunbeam Microplush Heated Throw Blanket
summary: The smartest way to turn stored battery power into warmth: on a power station, a heated throw keeps someone comfortable for hours on the energy a space heater would burn through in minutes.
verdict: Own a power station? In the cold, the most effective use for it is heating people rather than air. A heated throw such as Sunbeam's Microplush model puts warmth right against your body, under a blanket that also holds it in, and heated throws and blankets of this type typically draw well under 100 watts, often far less on low settings. Check the label on the one you buy. The gap is huge. A 1,500-watt space heater drains a 1kWh power station in well under an hour, while a heated throw drawing around 50 watts runs for most of a night on that same battery. Add a sleeping bag or a pile of comforters and you have a bed that stays warm even as the room slides into the 50s. Sunbeam throws include an auto shutoff for safety, which is good, though it means someone may wake up to restart it. Use it on top of you rather than folded or tucked under a mattress, and follow the manufacturer's instructions.
skipIf: Requires a power station, generator or some other AC source
pros: Uses a small fraction of the power a space heater pulls
Warms the person instead of the room, which is far more efficient
A mid-size power station can keep one going through a night
Earns its keep every winter, not only during outages
cons: Requires a power station, generator or some other AC source
Does nothing for the pipes or the room temperature
Auto shutoff timers may need resetting during the night

name: Coleman North Rim 0 Degree Mummy Sleeping Bag
summary: The cheapest and safest way to sleep warm in a cold house. Any household planning for winter outages should keep one cold-rated bag per person.
verdict: Few pieces of emergency heat gear are as underrated as a good sleeping bag. It burns nothing and draws nothing, and it turns your own body into the heat source. The Coleman North Rim is a widely sold synthetic mummy bag rated to 0 degrees Fahrenheit, far colder than the inside of a house gets in all but the longest outages. Read that number as a survival limit, not a comfort promise; most people are comfortable well above a bag's rated low. Indoors, that margin is exactly what you want. A family sleeping in cold-rated bags in one closed-off room can get through a night in the 40s with no heater at all, leaving a small propane heater to simply take the edge off in the evening. Put a foam pad or a mattress beneath the bag, because the floor draws heat away faster than air does. If a mummy bag feels too confining, a rectangular bag with a lower rating plus a wool blanket also works.
skipIf: Some sleepers find the mummy shape confining
pros: Requires no fuel, no electricity and no ventilation
The mummy hood holds heat around your head and shoulders
Rated for far colder conditions than an indoor room will reach
Serves as camping gear the rest of the year
cons: Some sleepers find the mummy shape confining
Synthetic fill takes up a lot of storage space
Temperature ratings assume ideal conditions; add layers if you sleep cold

name: Lasko 754200 Ceramic Space Heater
summary: Worth having only if you own a generator or a large home battery. On a typical portable power station, nothing wastes stored energy faster.
verdict: Part of the reason this heater is here is as a caution. The Lasko 754200 is a widely sold small ceramic heater with a 1,500-watt high setting, a lower setting, tip-over protection and an overheat cutoff. As an electric heater it is perfectly good. It is simply a poor partner for most battery backup. At 1,500 watts, a 1kWh power station lasts roughly 35 to 40 minutes once inverter losses are factored in, and the low setting adds only a little more time. It earns its place alongside a generator running outside, a whole-home battery system, or a large portable station that you can recharge from solar or a generator. Electric resistance heat gives off no combustion gases, a real advantage in a closed room, and a ceramic heater with tip-over protection is safer than any open flame. Plug it straight into the station or into a heavy-duty cord rated for the load, keep three feet of clearance from anything that can burn, and never leave it running unattended.
skipIf: Even on low, it empties a portable power station in hours or less
pros: Electric, so there is no combustion and no carbon monoxide
A low setting cuts the draw below the 1,500W maximum
Tip-over and overheat protection
Small, inexpensive and backed by a long track record
cons: Even on low, it empties a portable power station in hours or less
Only truly practical on a generator or a large home battery
Heats one small space and nothing more
